extracted.intended_audience: translators, satirical writers, and readers of Rabelais / literary satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for translating, prefacing, and producing satirical/lively prose (as exemplified by Rabelais), including tone choices for prefaces, fidelity vs. style in translation, and rhetorical devices that make satire effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface tone: two kinds (bully vs wheedle) and blending
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two sorts of taking prefaces ... Some, indeed, have bullied many of you into applause, and railed at your faults ... and others, more safely, have spoken kindly of you, that you might think ... favourably of them, and be flattered into patience. ... Why, then, truly I think on no other way at present but blending the two into one; and, from this marriage of huffing and cringing, there will result a new kind of careless medley, which, perhaps, will work upon both sorts of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a preface strategy aware of readership: aggressive 'railing' critics aim to bully into applause; gentle flattery aims to wheedle patience. If neither alone works for your audience, combine both approaches—mix forceful critique with strategic flatteries to reach different reader temperaments. Make the blend novel but not insincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific flattery beats general flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: flattery pleases you well when it is particular, you hate it, as little concerning you, when it is general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using flattering remarks (e.g., in a preface or endorsement), be specific about what you praise. Generic, sweeping praise is likely to be resented by readers; particular compliments feel genuine and persuade better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core qualities that recommend a satirical work
rubrics_metrics.description: If uncommon worth, lively wit, and deep learning, wove into wholesome satire, a bold, good, and vast design admirably pursued, truth set out in its true light, and a method how to arrive to its oracle, can recommend a work, I am sure this has enough to please any reasonable man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a combination of: substantial merit ('uncommon worth'), animated humor ('lively wit'), erudition ('deep learning'), moral/constructive satire ('wholesome satire'), ambitious coherent design ('bold... vast design'), truthful exposition, and a clear method or purpose. Presence of these elements makes satire broadly effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's primary responsibilities: convey sense and, when appropriate, copy style
rubrics_metrics.description: the first [translator's] praise, besides that of giving his author’s sense in its full extent, and copying his style, if it is to be copied; since he has no share in the invention or disposition of what he translates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize transferring the author's meaning fully; mimic the original's tone and style only when it serves the text. The translator is not an originator—faithful sense is paramount, and stylistic imitation is conditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation as creative labor: requires as much genius as invention
rubrics_metrics.description: to do the first well requires often as much genius as to do the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat translation as a creative, intellectual task. Good translation often demands as much skill and inventiveness as original composition—do not regard it as merely mechanical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulties of translating archaic/obscure phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: the obsolete words and turns of phrase, and dark subjects, often as darkly treated, make the sense hard to be understood even by a Frenchman, and it cannot be easy to give it the free easy air of an original
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating archaic language, aim to render sense into fresh, fluent prose without losing nuance. Modernize where necessary to achieve readability, but preserve the peculiarities that contribute to the original's comic or rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prize mere literal reproduction of cant or gibberish
rubrics_metrics.description: Far be it from me, for all this, to value myself upon hitting the words of cant in which my drolling author is so luxuriant; for though such words have stood me in good stead, I scarce can forbear thinking myself unhappy in having insensibly hoarded up so much gibberish and Billingsgate trash in my memory;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thinking that reproducing every slang term or obscene phrase verbatim is a virtue. Convey the impact, tone, and function of such language rather than mechanically transplanting it; unnecessary literalism can read as trashy or awkward in the target language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate author/creator bias and self-love among writers
rubrics_metrics.description: if thou art a brother of the quill, it is ten to one thou art too much in love with thy own dear productions to admire those of one of thy trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that writers (including translators) are likely to be partial to their own work. In evaluation, editing, or prefacing, account for authorial self-regard—seek external perspective and honest critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of learned parody, grand catalogue, and mythological allusion as comic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The preceding chapters lavish learned names, catalogues of uses, and mythological councils to praise the Pantagruelion (e.g., comparisons to gods, lists of uses across professions and nations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ erudite parody (mock-learned diction), exhaustive catalogues of absurd uses, and high-register mythological allusion to create comic contrast and satirical effect. Juxtaposing elevated style with ludicrous content amplifies humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extravagant hyperbole and mock-authority to produce comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The text ascribes absurdly grand virtues to a herb (e.g., makes it indispensable to all human arts, capable of launching voyages across zones, thwarting gods), and cites pseudo-scholarly experiments and authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exaggerated claims and faux-scholarly evidence as deliberate hyperbole. Presenting ridiculous assertions in the tone of authoritative discourse creates paradoxical humor and satirizes learned pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trope of inventor standing for the invention (figurative metonymy)
rubrics_metrics.description: they solecized and spoke improperly, unless you would excuse them by a trope, which alloweth us to posit the inventor in the place of the thing invented, as when Ceres is taken for bread, and Bacchus put instead of wine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage tropes such as metonymy (naming an invention by its inventor) for rhetorical play and comic economy. Such figurative switches can be used knowingly to create witty associations or ironies.
